modules.title: Why we do what we do

concepts.title: Habits
concepts.hook: One missed day did not reset habit growth in Lally's study; the fitted time to near full habit strength ran from 18 to 254 days.
concepts.rule: A cue can start a learned act. Repeating it in a stable setting can strengthen the cue link. In Lally and team’s study, time to near full habit strength varied a lot; one missed day did not wipe it out.

claims.text: Cues in a stable setting can bring back a learned action.
In Lally and team’s study, modeled times ranged from 18 to 254 days; one missed chance did not undo habit growth.

items.stem: Each day after hostel dinner, Nikhil reaches for a notebook on the same desk. What might start the action?

options.text: The familiar dinner-and-desk cue.
options.feedback: The repeated setting can bring back the learned act before he thinks much about a goal.

options.text: A magic fixed day count.
options.feedback: Repetition can build a cue link, but the study found no single deadline for everyone.

items.stem: During exam week, Tara misses one usual evening sketch. What does habit research suggest about that single gap?

options.text: One miss need not erase the learned link.
options.feedback: In the study, an occasional missed chance did not make earlier habit growth vanish.

options.text: The whole habit must return to zero.
options.feedback: A learned cue association builds over time and is not normally wiped by one missed act.

items.stem: A coach says every habit forms in 21 days. In Lally’s study, people varied widely. About how many days was the median fitted time to near-full automaticity?

options.text: 66 days.
options.feedback: The study’s median was 66 days, while individual fitted times varied from 18 to 254.

options.text: 21 days.
options.feedback: One fixed deadline misses the measured variation and does not match the study’s median.

items.stem: A student opens a music app after placing a bag on one hook. What is the likely cue in this example?

options.text: Seeing the bag on that hook.
options.feedback: The repeated place can become linked to the act even when the student's goal changes.

options.text: The total number of songs stored.
options.feedback: The library size says little about the repeated setting that precedes the action.

items.stem: A student keeps the same goal after moving rooms, yet starts a practiced action less often. Why could the move matter?

options.text: The old room’s cue may be absent.
options.feedback: The repeated setting can trigger the action; a new room may not provide that learned cue.

options.text: One new room resets every past repetition to zero.
options.feedback: Changing context may weaken a trigger, but it does not erase all prior practice.

items.stem: A cue appears, an act follows, and the link grows with repeats. The cue is part of the ___.

options.text: Setting that comes before the act.
options.feedback: Habits join a response to features of its usual context, such as place or prior action.

options.text: Reward promised after every attempt.
options.feedback: A cue can trigger the response even without a fresh reward at that moment.

items.stem: A student acts by habit after 21 days. A coach says every teammate will do the same by day 21. What is missing?

options.text: People and actions can vary widely.
options.feedback: One person’s timing cannot set a universal deadline; fitted times in the study spanned many weeks.

options.text: One example fixes the deadline for similar people.
options.feedback: The measured paths differed enough that one observed case cannot set the time for all.

items.stem: Put this familiar habit loop in a plausible order.

options.text: First: the usual cue appears.
options.feedback: The setting comes before the practiced response in this simple account of a habit.

options.text: Next: the learned response follows.
options.feedback: Repeated pairing can make the action follow the cue with less thought over time.

misconceptions.name: One fixed day count
misconceptions.correction: Habit time varies by person and act; there is no fixed day count.

misconceptions.name: One miss resets all
misconceptions.correction: One missed chance did not wipe out habit growth in the study.

sources.title: How are habits formed: Modelling habit formation in the real world
sources.publisher: Lally et al., European Journal of Social Psychology

sources.title: A new look at habits and the habit-goal interface

quest.title: Spot a cue
quest.detail: Watch one harmless daily act. Name the cue, the act, and the good result that may help it recur.

concepts.title: Loss aversion
concepts.hook: In classic choice experiments, the value curve is steeper for losses than for equal gains around a starting point.
concepts.rule: Loss aversion is a pattern where a loss can feel stronger than a same-size gain. It is a tendency in choices, not a law for every person or every case.

claims.text: Prospect theory treats gains and losses relative to a reference point.
Losses can weigh more than equal gains in choice.

items.stem: At a hostel game, Dev has ten tokens and loses one. How might that feel beside gaining one from ten?

options.text: The loss may feel stronger.
options.feedback: Prospect theory models changes from a starting point, with losses often carrying extra weight.

options.text: Both must feel exactly equal.
options.feedback: Equal token counts need not produce equal feelings when one change is framed as a loss.

items.stem: In a cricket pool, a student is handed ₹50, then asked to risk losing it for a chance at ₹50 more. Which pull may matter?

options.text: The possible loss of the held ₹50.
options.feedback: Once the amount feels owned, giving it up can weigh more than a same-size gain.

options.text: Only the possible gain can matter.
options.feedback: The starting point shapes the choice, so losing what is held can be a strong part.

items.stem: In a toy model of loss aversion, a 10-point loss feels twice as strong as a 10-point gain. About how many gained points would balance that loss in felt value?

options.text: 20 points.
options.feedback: In the stated toy model, a larger gain is needed to match the felt weight of the loss.

options.text: 10 points.
options.feedback: Equal point sizes do not balance felt value under the model’s stated loss aversion.

items.stem: A student hears the same final score framed as “keep five” or “lose five.” What changed?

options.text: The frame around the starting point.
options.feedback: A reference point can shift how a result is felt even if the arithmetic stays the same.

options.text: The number of points at stake.
options.feedback: Both lines mention five points; only their gain-or-loss wording changed.

items.stem: Two choices have the same final money, but one is framed as a loss from what a person holds. Why might they feel different?

options.text: The starting reference point changes the felt value.
options.feedback: A drop from what is held can weigh more than an equal gain from another starting point.

options.text: Equal final money forces equal felt value.
options.feedback: Prospect theory allows the framing of a change to matter even when final sums match.

items.stem: Prospect theory compares changes with a starting point. A move below it is framed as a ___.

options.text: Loss.
options.feedback: The reference point is key: the same final amount can be viewed through different frames.

options.text: Guaranteed gain.
options.feedback: Moving below a chosen start is the loss side of the comparison.

items.stem: A study group shows loss aversion on average. A coach predicts exactly twice the pain for every player. What is unsupported?

options.text: A group pattern is not one fixed personal ratio.
options.feedback: People differ. The study shows a common trend, not one set amount for every person.

options.text: A group average fixes each person’s response.
options.feedback: A group trend cannot tell us how each person feels about a loss.

items.stem: Match the change to its label from a ten-token start.

options.text: Ten to eleven
options.feedback: Moving above the start adds one token, so it belongs on the gain side.

options.text: A gain of one token
options.feedback: One extra token sits above the start, so its sign is positive in this example.

options.text: Ten to nine
options.feedback: The end count sits below the same start, making this a loss of one token.

options.text: A loss of one token
options.feedback: The number fell by one; its felt weight may still differ from an equal gain.

misconceptions.name: Equal feel
misconceptions.correction: Equal gain and loss can have a different felt weight.

misconceptions.name: Always true
misconceptions.correction: The pattern does not fix how every person will feel.

sources.title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk

quest.title: Frame a token
quest.detail: Write a made-up choice as a gain and then as a loss from a starting point. Ask how the frame may shift its feel.

concepts.title: Anchoring
concepts.hook: A random number can pull a later estimate: the first figure matters even when it has no link to the answer.
concepts.rule: An early number can pull a later guess toward it. That first number may be useful or random, so the guess needs a check beyond the anchor.

claims.text: A first number can pull a later guess toward it.
An anchor can pull a guess even when the first number is arbitrary.

items.stem: At a family shop, a tag first says ₹900 and then ₹600. What may shape a student's first price guess?

options.text: The ₹900 first number.
options.feedback: An early figure can pull a later judgment before any outside price is checked.

options.text: Only the ink colour.
options.feedback: The printed number gives a numeric starting point; colour does not explain the price estimate.

items.stem: On a train, two classmates guess the cost of a school trip. One first hears ₹2,000; the other hears ₹8,000. What might differ?

options.text: Their first guesses may be pulled apart.
options.feedback: Each guess can start near the first number heard. The numbers may have been made up.

options.text: Their guesses must match exactly.
options.feedback: Each first number can pull a guess its way. The two guesses need not match.

items.stem: In an anchoring study, one group saw a random 65% before guessing a percentage. About what median guess did that high-anchor group give?

options.feedback: The high anchor pulled the group median upward; the low-anchor group’s median was 25%.
That was the random starting anchor, not the group’s later median estimate.

items.stem: Which clue would test whether a marked-down pen is cheap?

options.text: A price for the same pen elsewhere.
options.feedback: A second shop's price gives a fresh clue that the first tag cannot give.

options.text: The crossed-out number alone.
options.feedback: That first number may be chosen by the seller and need not reflect a normal price.

items.stem: A school quiz shows a random 65 before asking for a percentage. Why might guesses still shift after students hear that it is random?

options.text: They may adjust from the first number.
options.feedback: The first number can pull later guesses, even when it gives no real clue.

options.text: A random number is a valid sample of the answer.
options.feedback: The number was picked at random. It tells us nothing about the true answer.

items.stem: A student guesses near a figure printed on a poster, then adjusts a little. That first figure is an ___.

options.text: Anchor.
options.feedback: The first number can tug a guess, even if the poster gives no real clue.

options.text: Independent check.
options.feedback: A number from the same prompt is the starting cue, not outside evidence.

items.stem: A seller crosses out ₹500 and asks ₹300. A buyer treats the old tag as independent proof of fair value. What is the flaw?

options.text: The seller may control that first number.
options.feedback: The crossed-out tag can anchor a guess without measuring the item’s value elsewhere.

options.text: The old tag independently checks the seller’s new tag.
options.feedback: Both numbers come from the same seller, so the first is not an outside comparison.

items.stem: Which line best sums up anchoring in a quiz?

options.text: An early number can tug a later guess.
options.feedback: Even a made-up first number can pull a later guess toward it.

options.text: The latest number always wins.
options.feedback: A later cue may matter too, but the bias concerns the pull of an initial figure.

misconceptions.name: First means fair
misconceptions.correction: The first number is not proof of the fair value.

misconceptions.name: Random has no pull
misconceptions.correction: Even an arbitrary first number can sway a later guess.

sources.title: Overcoming Cognitive Biases and Engaging in Critical Reflection
Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases

quest.title: Compare tags
quest.detail: Pick two made-up price tags. Start a guess from each, then see how the first number may pull the guess.

concepts.title: Confirmation bias
concepts.hook: In Wason's rule task, many people picked a card that could confirm the rule and skipped one that could break it.
concepts.rule: Confirmation bias is a pull to seek or notice clues that fit a belief. A fair test also looks for clues that could show the belief is wrong.

claims.text: People can focus on clues that fit a prior belief while missing other clues.
A test of an idea is stronger when it can find a case that goes against it.

items.stem: In exam week, Aditi thinks every hard paper hides a trick question. Which memory of hers shows this bias at work?

options.text: The one with a trick question.
options.feedback: A matching case fits her belief and may stand out more than a plain paper.

options.text: A paper with no trick question.
options.feedback: That counterexample could test her claim, but it does not match what she expects.

items.stem: A family shop owner thinks rain always cuts sales. What record would test the claim best?

options.text: Days with rain and steady sales too.
options.feedback: A possible exception can show whether the word “always” holds up across the records.

options.text: Only the wettest low-sales day.
options.feedback: One fitting day supports many stories and cannot rule out rain days with normal sales.

items.stem: In a Wason-style test, a rule could be checked by seeking a disconfirming card. About what percent in one nonthreatening-rule group chose the correct card pair?

options.feedback: Only a small share chose both cards needed to test the rule for a possible counterexample.
Most did not choose the pair that could expose a false rule in that study group.

items.stem: A cricket fan says a batter always fails in chases. Which scorecard matters most for checking “always”?

options.text: A successful chase innings.
options.feedback: One clear counterexample is enough to break a claim with the word “always.”

options.text: Another failed chase innings.
options.feedback: More matches in line with the belief cannot by themselves rule out successful chases.

items.stem: A rule predicts that every late bus is red. Why is checking a late bus that is not red useful?

options.text: It could disprove the universal rule.
options.feedback: A red late bus fits the rule, but one late bus of another colour would break it.

options.text: Another red bus is the only decisive test.
options.feedback: More matching cases cannot rule out the counterexample that the claim forbids.

items.stem: A student saves only screenshots that support her guess. She is filtering evidence toward ___.

options.text: Her existing belief.
options.feedback: The pattern can make a weak idea seem stronger by hiding cases that point away.

options.text: A random mix of all cases.
options.feedback: Selective saving changes the sample, so the folder no longer shows the full record.

items.stem: A student saves three bus logs that fit her belief and skips two that do not. She calls the belief proven. What is the flaw?

options.text: The saved sample leaves out contrary cases.
options.feedback: Selecting only matches can make a weak belief look stronger than the full record supports.

options.text: Three saved logs outweigh every omitted log.
options.feedback: The omitted records may directly challenge the claim, regardless of how many matches were saved.

items.stem: How can a student miss clues against a belief?

options.text: We may notice support and miss possible exceptions.
options.feedback: The bias lies in uneven search or recall, regardless of whether the starting idea is true.

options.text: It means all facts we like are lies.
options.feedback: The facts in favour may be real. Yet left-out cases can change the picture.

misconceptions.name: One match proves it
misconceptions.correction: One fitting case may fit more than one idea.

misconceptions.name: Disproof is useless
misconceptions.correction: A case against an idea can test it well.

sources.title: Motivated Reasoning and Performance on the Wason Selection Task
sources.publisher: Dawson, Gilovich and Regan, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

quest.title: Try to disprove
quest.detail: Pick a low-stakes belief about a game or bus. Write one clue that could show it is wrong.

concepts.title: Social proof
concepts.hook: In Asch's line task, a plainly wrong group answer still pulled some participants away from what they saw.
concepts.rule: A crowd choice can act as a clue and pull a person’s choice. But a crowd can be wrong; group agreement is not proof.

claims.text: In Asch’s line task, group answers sometimes pulled a person toward a wrong answer.
Group agreement is social input, not proof that a claim is true.

items.stem: At a hostel quiz, most students pick the wrong line length aloud. What may happen to the last student's answer?

options.text: It may move toward the group choice.
options.feedback: A public majority can change some answers even when the visual task seems clear.

options.text: It must stay fully independent.
options.feedback: Some people in the study did follow a group answer, even when it was wrong.

items.stem: During a cricket watch party, everyone cheers a disputed call before the replay. What might the crowd signal do?

options.text: Make the call seem more certain.
options.feedback: The cheers come first. They can sway a guess before the replay gives a clear view.

options.text: Prove the call was right.
options.feedback: Shared confidence does not replace the replay or make the first judgment accurate.

items.stem: In Asch’s line task, a group gave wrong answers aloud. About what percent of critical answers from the lone participant followed the wrong group?

options.text: About 37%.
options.feedback: Asch reported 36.8% wrong answers on critical trials, showing a strong group pull.

options.text: About 1%.
options.feedback: That was closer to the error rate without group pressure, not the critical group trials.

items.stem: A whole class picks the same answer to an easy line puzzle. What does that show by itself?

options.text: Agreement, not proof of accuracy.
options.feedback: The group may share a mistake, so a headcount alone cannot settle the visual fact.

options.text: The answer is certainly right.
options.feedback: Many votes can point the same way even when the compared lines say otherwise.

items.stem: A student sees a clear line match but publicly follows a wrong group answer. Why can this happen?

options.text: Fitting in can outweigh a private judgment.
options.feedback: In Asch’s task, public group pressure could pull answers away from the visible line lengths.

options.text: Unanimity makes the wrong line physically longer.
options.feedback: The lines do not change; the social setting can change what a person says aloud.

items.stem: If a crowd's visible choice nudges a person's own choice, the crowd is serving as a ___.

options.text: Social cue.
options.feedback: The signal comes from what others did, though its size does not make it reliable.

options.text: Private measurement.
options.feedback: A group vote is shared behaviour, not an independent check of the object.

items.stem: A group chooses B before anyone checks the evidence. A student calls their unanimous votes independent proof. What is missing?

options.text: Their votes may influence one another.
options.feedback: A shared answer can spread through a group, so agreement alone is not a fresh check.

options.text: Unanimous votes guarantee independent checks.
options.feedback: One group answer can spread to others. The votes need not come from separate checks.

items.stem: Which explanation fits the line-length result in Asch's task?

options.text: A wrong majority sometimes shifted individual answers.
options.feedback: The finding shows influence in that setting, while people did not all copy every time.

options.text: Every participant copied on every trial.
options.feedback: The effect was real but varied across people and trials rather than being universal.

misconceptions.name: Crowd proves truth
misconceptions.correction: A group can agree on a wrong answer.

misconceptions.name: No one is swayed
misconceptions.correction: Group answers can pull some people in some settings.

quest.title: Watch a group cue
quest.detail: In a harmless choice, note whether a visible group choice changes a guess. Keep the check kind.

concepts.title: The planning fallacy
concepts.hook: In a study, students thought their papers would take less time than they did. Even their best guesses ran short.
concepts.rule: The planning fallacy is a tilt toward a short time guess for our own task. Looking at past tasks and missed steps can give a better time guess.

claims.text: People can underguess how long their own tasks will take.
Plans can miss delays that happened in similar past work.

items.stem: A hostel team says its chart will take one hour but has not counted printing. What might happen?

options.text: It may take longer than guessed.
options.feedback: Missing a step from the imagined path can make the finish time estimate too short.

options.text: It must finish in one hour.
options.feedback: A stated estimate does not print the pages or remove other uncounted work.

items.stem: During exam week, Isha plans a revision sheet and forgets to gather past papers. Which estimate is at risk?

options.text: Her own finish-time guess.
options.feedback: The missing collection step adds work outside the smooth path she pictured.

options.text: The length of every past paper.
options.feedback: Forgetting a step affects her plan duration, not the printed size of old papers.

items.stem: A club plans posters in 2 hours but forgot printing. Similar past posters took 3, 4, and 5 hours. About how many hours does the past-task view suggest?

options.text: 4 hours.
options.feedback: Past completed jobs give a four-hour comparison point that includes steps the new plan missed.

options.text: 2 hours.
options.feedback: That repeats the plan despite the missing printing step and the longer past tasks.

items.stem: A student lists only drawing time for a project. What overlooked step could add time?

options.text: Finding and printing source images.
options.feedback: The work also needs images and print time. A drawing-only count leaves those out.

options.text: The colour of a finished poster.
options.feedback: A finished colour is a feature of output, not a missing step in the schedule.

items.stem: A team imagines a smooth poster project and ignores likely printing delays. Why can its time guess run short?

options.text: The plan leaves out a common work step.
options.feedback: The imagined best case omits printing time that similar real tasks may include.

options.text: A smooth plan makes unlisted steps take no time.
options.feedback: Missing work still takes time even when the planned steps go smoothly.

items.stem: To compare a new task with old ones, the useful number is the time those old tasks ___.

options.text: Actually took.
options.feedback: Old jobs show the time used, with snags and steps the new plan may miss.

options.text: Were first hoped to take.
options.feedback: An earlier wish may repeat the same optimism instead of showing the work's duration.

items.stem: Past posters took four to six hours. A new plan says one hour because artwork is ready, but printing is uncounted. What is weak?

options.text: The guess omits a step and dismisses past times.
options.feedback: Ready artwork may help, yet the past tasks and missing printing step still matter.

options.text: Ready artwork proves all other steps vanish.
options.feedback: One completed part cannot establish the time for all remaining work.

items.stem: Which sentence sums up the planning fallacy in a school project?

options.text: A smooth imagined path can understate real time.
options.feedback: Past completed jobs can reveal delays that a new plan has not pictured.

options.text: Every late job was planned badly.
options.feedback: The pattern concerns biased time guesses, not a verdict on every team or task.

misconceptions.name: Best case is normal
misconceptions.correction: A smooth plan is only one path; delays can add time.

misconceptions.name: Past tasks do not help
misconceptions.correction: Past task times can show steps a new plan has missed.

sources.title: Exploring the Planning Fallacy: Why People Underestimate Their Task Completion Times
sources.publisher: Buehler, Griffin and Ross, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

quest.title: Time a small task
quest.detail: Before a small school task, note a time guess. Afterward, note the time and one step the guess missed.
